In the cloud (incl. EU data residency)

Source: vignettes/articles/install-cloud.Rmd
install-cloud.Rmd

The deployment needs nothing provider-specific: a Linux virtual machine, or a Kubernetes cluster, from any provider will do. This guide says what to ask a provider for, how the installation differs from the cluster guide, and what to check when the data must stay in the EU. It names no provider. The single-VM path was tested on a Civo instance in London with Ubuntu 24.04.

Two ways to run it

A. One virtual machine with K3s. The simplest. Everything, including the database, runs on one VM; the cluster guide applies step by step. You need:

  • a VM with 8 or more vCPUs, 16 to 32 GB of memory and 100 GB of disk, running Ubuntu 24.04 or Rocky Linux 9;
  • a public IP address, or a private one reached through your network;
  • a firewall that allows SSH (22) from your own address only, and HTTP (80) and HTTPS (443) from the users’ networks;
  • a hostname for the IP (an A record, or a name such as 1-2-3-4.sslip.io for a test).

B. A managed Kubernetes cluster. The provider runs the control plane and supplies storage and load balancers. Use the cluster guide from step 4, with these differences:

  • Skip the K3s install and coredns.yml. The hostname resolves through DNS.
  • The cluster needs a default StorageClass that provides ReadWriteOnce volumes. PostgreSQL asks for 20 GB and Dex for 1 GB.
  • traefik.yml exposes Traefik as a LoadBalancer Service. The provider creates a load balancer with an external IP; point the hostname’s A record at it (kubectl -n immunoplex get svc shows the IP).
  • The i-spi-compute worker image is built for amd64: the worker needs amd64 nodes, and its nodeSelector asks for them.
  • Give the node pool enough room for the worker’s limits (2 CPUs and 4 GB in the manifest; raise them for real studies, see Overview).

A managed PostgreSQL service can replace the bundled one: point I-SPI’s db_* and the worker’s DB_* variables at it, keep TLS required, and load the schema from db/ into it. This is not tested here.

TLS

Each Ingress has the annotation cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: intermediate-ca1-issuer. On a cloud host you can choose:

  • The private certificate authority from the cluster guide. Browsers trust the site only after importing its root certificate. Acceptable for a closed group of users.

  • An ACME issuer, such as Let’s Encrypt. Browsers trust it without any import. The hostname must be public and reachable on port 80 for the HTTP-01 challenge. Create a ClusterIssuer for it, then point the Ingresses at it:

    sed -i "s/cluster-issuer: intermediate-ca1-issuer/cluster-issuer: <your-issuer>/" *.yml

    Traefik here watches only the immunoplex namespace, which is also where cert-manager places the challenge solver for these certificates. This combination has not been tested; check that the first certificate is issued (kubectl -n immunoplex get certificate).

  • Your organisation’s certificates. Create a cert-manager issuer for your CA, or store the certificate as the Secret cert-secret that the Ingresses use.

Keeping the data in the EU

These points concern where the data and its copies are stored and processed. They are technical checks, not legal advice; your data protection officer decides what the data requires.

  • Region. Create the VM or cluster, its disks and its load balancer in an EU region. With managed Kubernetes, also check where the control plane runs.
  • What holds personal or study data. The PostgreSQL volume (all assay data and results) and Dex’s volume (user accounts and email addresses). The Redis queue holds job descriptions only while they run. I-SPI, the API and the worker keep no data of their own.
  • Backups and snapshots. Database dumps, volume snapshots and VM images are copies of the data: keep them in the same region, or another EU region. Check the provider’s default for snapshot and backup location.
  • Logs. Pod logs contain user email addresses and study names. If the provider ships logs to a central service, check where it stores them.
  • Images. The images contain software, not data, and can come from any registry. To avoid depending on registries outside the EU at run time, copy the images into a registry in the same region and change the image: fields; the image list is in Without internet access.
  • Sign-in. Dex stores accounts in the cluster itself; no external identity service is involved unless you configure one.
  • Access. Restrict SSH and the Kubernetes API to your own addresses, and keep the configured manifests, which hold the secrets, out of version control.

Cost and time

  • One VM in the 8 vCPU, 16 to 32 GB range costs a few units of currency per day at most providers. Stop or delete it when a test is over: deleting the VM deletes the data with it, so pg_dump first if you want to keep results.
  • Allow 30 to 60 minutes from a new VM to a working sign-in: a few minutes to create the VM, about 10 for K3s and cert-manager, and the rest for pulling images and starting pods.
